title: A Concrete PRG: Hard-Core Predicates, the BMY Construction, and BBS

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 2.5 (hard-core predicates, BMY, BBS); ln00a Ch. 2.3

body:
## The goal: turn one-wayness into pseudorandomness

Theorem 2.14 (previous lesson) says pseudorandom generators exist if and only if one-way functions exist. The easy direction is a three-line reduction; the hard direction — build a PRG from an *arbitrary* one-way function — is the deep HILL construction. But there is a clean, fully-understood special case that already delivers a concrete, implementable generator: assume the one-way function is 1-1 and length-preserving (a permutation), attach one hard-core bit, iterate, and you get **BBS**. This lesson builds that special case from first principles.

## Why a one-way function alone is not enough

One-wayness says only that *inverting* is hard. It says nothing about partial information: for $f'(x,r)=(f(x),r)$, the string $r$ appears verbatim in the output, so half the input leaks, yet $f'$ is one-way whenever $f$ is. Pseudorandomness needs the opposite — a *single bit of the input that no efficient algorithm can guess from the output*. That is a hard-core predicate.

@def:hardcore

Three facts shape the definition:

- **Trivial guessers already win half the time** — a random bit is correct with probability exactly $1/2$. The definition only forbids non-negligible *advantage* over $1/2$.
- **A hard-core is almost unbiased** — a biased predicate is beaten by the constant "majority bit" predictor.
- **For 1-1 $f$, hard-core $\implies$ one-way** — an inverter of $f$ would predict $b(x)$ from $f(x)$ by inverting and then evaluating $b$. So a hard-core is strictly stronger (Exercise 2).

A predicate can be hard-core for the trivial reason that $f$ discards information (e.g. $f(\sigma,x)=(0,x')$ has hard-core $\sigma$). The interesting case is 1-1 $f$, where the hardness is purely computational. Does every one-way function have a hard-core? Goldreich–Levin says yes.

@thm:thm211

In words: given $f(x)$ and a random mask $r$, guessing the parity $\langle x,r\rangle$ is hard. Appending the mask turns *any* one-way function into one with a hard-core, so the theory never runs out of examples.

## Step 1: one hard bit $\to$ one extra output bit (Proposition 2.12)

@thm:prop212

**The reduction in one paragraph.** Since $f$ is a permutation, $f(U_n)$ is uniform, so $U_{n+1}$ is distributed exactly as $f(U_n)$ followed by a fresh random bit. It therefore suffices to show $f(s)b(s)$ is indistinguishable from $f(s)$ followed by a random bit. A distinguisher between these two, fed $f(s)$ with a random $\beta$ appended, decides whether $\beta=b(s)$ better than chance — and that is precisely a predictor of $b(s)$ given $f(s)$. Contradiction. (The full "distinguisher $\implies$ predictor" template is Exercise 1; the theorem's proof fills in the arithmetic.)

## Step 2: stretch to any polynomial length (BMY, Eq. 2.9)

Proposition 2.12 buys one extra bit. Iterate $f$ and harvest one hard-core bit per round:

@thm:bmy

Security is argued **right to left**. An adversary who predicts $b(x_i)$ from the later bits $b(x_{i+1}),\dots,b(x_{\ell-1})$ can, given $y=f(x_i)$, compute those later bits itself — iterating $f$ forward from $y$ — and thereby predict $b(x_i)$ from $f(x_i)$, contradicting the hard-core property. Together with Yao's equivalence (next-bit unpredictability $\iff$ pseudorandomness, @def:unpredictable), this makes the iterated generator a PRG. Conclusion: a 1-1, length-preserving one-way function implies PRGs of every polynomial stretch.

## The concrete instance: BBS

Instantiate the skeleton with a specific, implementable permutation — modular squaring modulo a Blum integer.

@def:blum-integer

@thm:bbs

**Practical notes.**

- The seed is the state size: $k=256$–$1024$ bits is typical (matched to the security level of factoring). The stretch $\ell(k)$ may be any polynomial.
- BBS is slow — one modular squaring per output bit — but its value is provable security: no statistical test beats it unless factoring is easy.
- The same skeleton with $f$ = modular exponentiation and $b$ = the most significant bit gives the **Blum–Micali** generator, based on the discrete-logarithm problem.

## Why this matters

- **The hybrid argument appears twice** — once in Proposition 2.12 (distinguishing $b(s)$ from random is distinguishing $b(s)$ from $1-b(s)$), once in Yao's equivalence (hybrids over prefixes). This is the payoff of M3: the technique that turns one hard bit into a whole pseudorandom stream.
- **BBS closes the loop of Chapter 2**: definitions (M2) $\to$ technique (M3) $\to$ construction (M4). You now hold a complete, provably secure PRG built from first principles.
- **It demystifies "cryptographically secure randomness"**: the generator's security is a *theorem* reducible to factoring, not a heuristic — the standard every CSPRNG is held to.

defs.name: Hard-core predicate (Definition 2.10)
defs.statement:
A polynomial-time computable predicate $b:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}$ is a **hard-core** of a function $f$ if for every probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm $A'$, every positive polynomial $p(\cdot)$, and all sufficiently large $n$:

$$\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}[A'(f(x))=b(x)] < \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{p(n)}.$$

Equivalently, given $f(x)$, no efficient algorithm predicts $b(x)$ non-negligibly better than a coin flip.
defs.intuition: The strongest useful notion of "unpredictable bit": you cannot even learn one designated bit of $x$, only its image. For 1-1 $f$ this is strictly stronger than one-wayness.

defs.name: Blum integer and the modular-squaring function
defs.statement:
Let $p\equiv q\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ be large primes and set $N=pq$; such an $N$ is a **Blum integer**. Let $QR_N=\{x^2\bmod N : x\in\mathbb Z_N^*\}$ be the quadratic residues. Modular squaring

$$f(x)=x^2\bmod N\qquad(x\in QR_N)$$

is a **permutation of $QR_N$**: every quadratic residue has exactly one square root that is itself a residue (this is what $p\equiv q\equiv 3\pmod 4$ forces). Inverting $f$ — extracting square roots mod $N$ — is polynomial-time equivalent to factoring $N$ (Rabin), so $f$ is a *candidate* one-way function: one-way assuming factoring is hard, a standard but unproven assumption.
defs.intuition: The congruence condition makes squaring a 1-1 map on $QR_N$ (density $\approx 1/4$ of the $n$-bit strings) — exactly the permutation hypothesis the BMY construction needs — and gives the BBS sequence a clean, purely periodic structure.

defs.name: Next-bit unpredictability (Yao's theorem)
defs.statement: An ensemble $\{Z_k\}$ is **next-bit unpredictable** if every probabilistic polynomial-time machine, given a prefix of $Z_k$, predicts the next bit with probability non-negligibly better than $1/2$. **Yao's theorem:** a polynomial-time constructible ensemble is pseudorandom if and only if it is next-bit unpredictable.
defs.intuition: A stream looks random exactly when each bit is a surprise given the past. The hybrid argument shows this local property is equivalent to the global one (indistinguishability from uniform).

theorems.name: Theorem 2.11 (Goldreich–Levin): a generic hard-core
theorems.statement: For any one-way function $f$, define $g(x,r)=(f(x),r)$ with $|x|=|r|$, and let $b(x,r)=\langle x,r\rangle$ denote the inner product of $x$ and $r$ modulo 2. Then $g$ is one-way, and $b$ is a hard-core predicate of $g$ (not of $f$).
theorems.intuition: Every one-way function can be modified to have a hard-core, so hard-core-based constructions are fully general. The key point is that the hard-core is of $g=(f,r)$, not of $f$ itself.
theorems.proof:
Proof (sketch). *(1) Amplification.* Since $A'$ has advantage $\varepsilon$ over random $(x,r)$, a Chebyshev argument shows that for at least an $\varepsilon/2$ fraction of $x$'s, the machine $A'_x(r)=A'(f(x),r)$ predicts $b(x,r)$ with probability $\ge \tfrac12+\tfrac\varepsilon2$ over random $r$; call these "good" $x$.

*(2) Reconstruction.* For a good $x$ we recover $x$ bit by bit. To find the $j$-th bit $x_j$, pick $t=\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$ pairwise-independent strings $r_1,\dots,r_t$; for each $i$ query $A'$ on both $(f(x),r_i)$ and $(f(x),r_i\oplus e_j)$ to obtain guesses for $b(x,r_i)$ and $b(x,r_i\oplus e_j)$. Since $b(x,r_i\oplus e_j)=b(x,r_i)\oplus x_j$, the XOR of the two guesses is a vote for $x_j$ that is correct with probability $\tfrac12+\Omega(\varepsilon^2)$; a majority over the pairwise-independent $r_i$'s (Chebyshev) then fixes $x_j$ with high probability. Doing this for every $j$ inverts $f$ on every good $x$ — a non-negligible fraction of inputs — contradicting one-wayness. ∎

theorems.name: Proposition 2.12: a simple PRG from a hard-core
theorems.statement:
Let $b$ be a hard-core predicate of a polynomial-time computable, 1-1, length-preserving function $f$. Then

$$G(s)=f(s)\,b(s)$$

is a pseudorandom generator, stretching $n$ bits to $n+1$ bits.
theorems.intuition: One unpredictable bit per evaluation of $f$. The reduction "distinguisher $\implies$ predictor" is the template behind every hard-core construction.
theorems.proof:
Since $f$ is 1-1 and length-preserving it is a permutation of $\{0,1\}^n$, so the $n$-bit prefix $f(U_n)$ of $G(U_n)$ is uniform. Hence $U_{n+1}$ has the same distribution as $f(U_n)$ followed by a fresh random bit $U_1$; it remains only to show that appending $b(s)$ is as good as appending a random bit, i.e. that $f(s)b(s)$ is indistinguishable from $f(s)\circ U_1$.

Suppose a PPT $D$ distinguishes $\{G(U_n)\}$ from $\{U_{n+1}\}$ with gap exceeding $1/p(n)$. Since $U_{n+1}=f(U_n)b(U_n)$ with probability $1/2$ and $=f(U_n)\bar b(U_n)$ otherwise (writing $\bar b=1-b$), this gap gives

$$\Pr[D(f(U_n)b(U_n)){=}1]-\Pr[D(f(U_n)\bar b(U_n)){=}1] > \tfrac{2}{p(n)}$$

(if the sign is reversed, negate $D$). Build a predictor $A$ for $b$: on input $y=f(x)$, pick $\beta\in\{0,1\}$ uniformly, run $D(y\beta)$, and output $\beta$ if $D$ accepts and $1-\beta$ otherwise. Then, with $U_1$ denoting the random $\beta$,

$$\Pr[A(f(U_n))=b(U_n)] = \Pr[D(f(U_n)U_1){=}1\wedge U_1{=}b(U_n)] + \Pr[D(f(U_n)U_1){=}0\wedge 1{-}U_1{=}b(U_n)]$$

$$= \tfrac12\Pr[D(f(U_n)b(U_n)){=}1] + \tfrac12\big(1-\Pr[D(f(U_n)\bar b(U_n)){=}1]\big) = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\big(\Pr[D(fb){=}1]-\Pr[D(f\bar b){=}1]\big) > \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{p(n)},$$

contradicting that $b$ is a hard-core of $f$. ∎

theorems.name: BMY construction (Eq. 2.9): arbitrary polynomial stretch
theorems.statement:
Let $f$ be a 1-1, length-preserving one-way function with hard-core $b$, and let $\ell$ be any polynomial. Set $x_0=s$ and $x_i=f(x_{i-1})$. Then

$$G(s)=b(x_0)b(x_1)\cdots b(x_{\ell(|s|)-1}) = b(s)b(f(s))\cdots b(f^{\ell(|s|)-1}(s))$$

(where $f^i$ denotes the $i$-fold iterate) is a pseudorandom generator of stretch $\ell(|s|)$.
theorems.intuition: Iterate the one-way function, harvesting one hard-core bit per step. Each bit is fresh randomness because knowing all later bits still does not reveal the current one.
theorems.proof:
*Right-to-left unpredictability.* We show $G(U_k)$ is next-bit unpredictable read right to left, i.e. that the reversed string $b(x_{\ell-1})\cdots b(x_0)$ is unpredictable. Suppose a predictor, given the suffix $b(x_{i+1})\cdots b(x_{\ell-1})$, predicts $b(x_i)$ with advantage $\varepsilon$. Given $y=f(x_i)$ we can compute $x_{i+1}=f(x_i)$, then $x_{i+2},\dots,x_{\ell-1}$ — all forward, deterministically — and evaluate the polynomial-time predicate $b$ on each to obtain the suffix. Feeding it to the predictor predicts $b(x_i)$ from $f(x_i)$ with advantage $\varepsilon$, contradicting that $b$ is a hard-core of $f$. The reversal is essential: the reduction can only iterate $f$ *forward* from the given $y=f(x_i)$, so it can supply the *suffix* (later bits), turning "predict the previous bit" into "predict $b$ of the current value".

*Yao's equivalence.* Unpredictability implies pseudorandomness by a hybrid argument. For an ensemble $Z$ of $m$-bit strings, define the $(i{+}1)$-st hybrid as the first $i$ bits of $Z$ followed by $m-i$ uniform bits; the extremes are $Z$ and $U_m$, so a distinguisher with gap $\varepsilon$ separates some neighboring pair with gap $\ge \varepsilon/m$ (average argument). Neighboring hybrids differ only in the $(i{+}1)$-st bit — true versus random — so a distinguisher for that pair is exactly a next-bit predictor with advantage $\varepsilon/m$. Hence next-bit unpredictability $\iff$ pseudorandomness. ∎

theorems.name: BBS: the Blum–Blum–Shub generator
theorems.statement:
Let $N$ be a Blum integer. Choose a random seed $s\in\mathbb Z_N^*$, set $x_0=s^2\bmod N$, and iterate $x_{i+1}=x_i^2\bmod N$, outputting

$$G(s)=\mathrm{LSB}(x_0),\;\mathrm{LSB}(x_1),\;\mathrm{LSB}(x_2),\dots$$

(the first $\ell(|s|)$ bits for a stretch function $\ell$). Assuming factoring $N$ (equivalently, extracting square roots mod $N$) is hard, the least significant bit is a hard-core of modular squaring (Alexi–Chor–Goldreich–Schnorr 1988; Vazirani–Vazirani 1985). By the BMY analysis, $G$ is therefore a pseudorandom generator.
theorems.intuition: A concrete, implementable PRG whose security is a theorem: any next-bit predictor would be a factoring algorithm.
theorems.proof:
Two pieces, both already in place.

1. **LSB is a hard-core of squaring, under the factoring assumption.** Given $y=x^2\bmod N$ with $x\in QR_N$, an LSB oracle recovers $x$ bit by bit — query the oracle on $(x\cdot 2^{-j})^2\bmod N$ to learn the $j$-th bit of $x$ — with the $\pm$ ambiguity resolved by the Blum structure (each residue has a unique residue square root). Holding a square root $x'$ of $y$, with probability $1/2$ we have $x'\neq\pm x$, and then $\gcd(x-x',N)$ is a nontrivial factor of $N$. So a next-bit predictor for BBS would factor $N$.

2. **BMY then applies.** Squaring is a permutation of $QR_N$ (a set of density $\approx 1/4$ among $n$-bit strings), so it meets the permutation hypothesis of the BMY construction up to constant-factor bookkeeping; instantiating BMY with $f$ = squaring and $b$ = LSB yields exactly $G$. ∎

checkpoints.question: Why is a one-way function alone not enough to build a PRG, and what does a hard-core predicate add?

options.text: One-wayness only says inverting is hard; it allows easy partial information about x (e.g. f′(x,r) = (f(x),r) leaks all of r). A hard-core b guarantees a specific bit of x is unpredictable from f(x) — the raw material a PRG outputs.
One-way functions are too slow to evaluate, so we need a faster primitive.
A hard-core predicate is the same as a one-way function, just written differently.
One-wayness only holds for 1-1 functions, and PRGs need general functions.

checkpoints.explanation: One-wayness is an inverting guarantee; it says nothing about whether f(x) leaks bits of x. The example f′(x,r) = (f(x),r) shows a perfectly one-way function can reveal half its input verbatim. A hard-core predicate is the strongest 'one bit stays secret' guarantee, and it is exactly the ingredient G(s) = f(s)∘b(s) / BMY harvests to produce pseudorandom bits.

checkpoints.question: In the proof of Prop 2.12, why is it enough to show f(s)b(s) is indistinguishable from f(s)∘(random bit)?

options.text: Because f is 1-1 and length-preserving, f(U_n) alone is already uniform, so U_{n+1} ≡ f(U_n) followed by a random bit — the only question left is whether the appended bit is as good as random.
Because the distinguisher is only allowed to look at the last bit.
Because b(s) is independent of f(s) by definition of hardness.
Because Prop 2.6 already proves indistinguishability survives appending bits.

checkpoints.explanation: Since f is a permutation of {0,1}^n, the prefix f(U_n) of G(U_n) is perfectly uniform, so replacing the appended bit by a uniform bit is the entire security question: U_{n+1} is exactly f(U_n) with a fresh random last bit. The proof then shows 'detecting the swap' is exactly 'predicting b(s) from f(s)'.

checkpoints.question: Why does the BMY construction argue unpredictability from right to left?

options.text: The reduction must compute forward from the given y = f(x_i): it can produce x_{i+1},…,x_{ℓ−1} and their hard-core bits (the suffix), but not x_{i−1}. Reading right-to-left turns 'predict the previous bit' into 'predict b of the current value', which contradicts hard-coreness.
Because f is only one-way when applied from right to left.
Because LSB is only a hard-core when read from right to left.
It is a notational convention with no computational content.

checkpoints.explanation: The predictor in the reduction is handed y = f(x_i) and must reconstruct the context a next-bit predictor would have seen. It can only iterate f forward (x_{i+1} = f(x_i), etc.), so the bits it can produce are b(x_{i+1}),…,b(x_{ℓ−1}) — the suffix. Hence the unpredictability claim must be about predicting the previous bit from the suffix, i.e. unpredictability of the reversed string.

exercises.prompt: Write the full reduction in Prop 2.12: given a distinguisher D between G(U_n) = f(U_n)b(U_n) and U_{n+1}, construct the predictor A of b(U_n) from f(U_n) and verify the probability calculation that A succeeds with probability > 1/2 + 1/p(n).
exercises.hint: A on input y: pick β uniformly, run D(yβ), output β if D accepts, else 1−β. Split the success probability into the two cases U₁ = b(U_n) and U₁ ≠ b(U_n); recall Pr[U_{n+1} = f(U_n)b(U_n)] = 1/2 because f is a permutation.

exercises.prompt: Prove: if b is a hard-core of a polynomial-time computable 1-1 function f, then f is one-way. (This justifies the claim that hard-coreness is strictly stronger than one-wayness.)
exercises.hint: Assume an inverter I finds a preimage of f(x) with non-negligible probability. Since f is 1-1 the preimage is unique — use I to predict b(x).

exercises.prompt: BBS warm-up: let N = 7·11 = 77 (a Blum integer, since 7 ≡ 11 ≡ 3 mod 4). Take seed s = 3, so x₀ = s² mod N = 9. Compute the first 6 bits of the BBS sequence (x_{i+1} = x_i² mod 77, output the LSB of each x_i). Then explain why the initial state is s² mod N rather than s itself.
exercises.hint: Squaring the state: 9 → 4 → 16 → 25 → 9 → 4. The state orbit has period 4, so the LSB sequence repeats with period 4. For the second part: squaring once moves the state into QR_N, the domain on which squaring is a permutation.
